newsitem.title: UK: Baht contagion to stay regional - London analysts.
newsitem.headline: Baht contagion to stay regional - London analysts.

text.p: The effective devaluation of the Thai baht early Wednesday sent ripples of instability around south east Asian markets but traders in Europe said they expect any contagion to be contained there for now.

Emerging market investors have become more selective in assessing individual currency risks and beyond the obvious regional effects of the baht slide on relative export competitiveness the investment environment remains calm in other developing markets.

"The contagion is going to be limited. For a start, the global environment is different from May and investors' risk appetite is higher," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at JP Morgan Europe.

"Back in May, problems in these markets were exaggerated by concerns about U.S. and Japanese interest rates going up, the strengthening yen and the repayment of a significant amount of yen borrowings. That's not the case at the moment."
The Thai authorities weathered an attack on the baht in May by reimposing foreign exchange controls and effectively creating a two-tier baht market for domestic and overseas players.

The Czech Republic faced a simultaneous attack on the crown. But, after a brief period with exchange controls, its abandoned its currency peg in favour of a managed float and allowed the crown to weaken by about 10 percent.
One explanation for the timing of the two crises in May, apart from fundamental weakness of their current accounts, had been jitters about global interest rates and a rising yen.
Many plays in high-yielding emerging markets were funded by cheap yen borrowings over the past two years and these positions were being squeezed by the threat of higher Japanese rates.

On Wednesday, Baht traded offshore slumped about 18 percent to about 29 per dollar after the Thai central bank said it too was adopting a managed flotation of the currency in place of its previous peg to a heavily dollar-weighted basket.

The competitive edge that a weaker baht gives Thai exports has put pressure on its major regional trading partners and selling of the Indonesian rupiah, Malaysia ringgit and Philippines peso was evident in the immediate aftermath today.

"The contagion seems to be more regional now because it's often the same investors who are in a particular region and if you get burned on one you begin to worry about some of the others," said Nick Douch, corporate risk adviser at BZW.
But, beyond that, analysts said it is hard to see any obvious reason for jitters extending elsewhere to eastern Europe, South Africa or Latin America, they said.
"This should remain a local or at best a regional story," said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS.
"There maybe some spin-offs in Indonesia, Malaysia and possibly the Philippines, as these countries have lost significant competitiveness, but this is not another Mexico."

Some said the relative stability of the Czech crown since its 10 percent devaluation last month may have encouraged the Thai authorities to go the same route today but some analysts said this was a risky parallel to draw.

The Czech central bank has only fostered stability of the crown at the expense of punitive interest rates, which will only exaggerate the economic slowdown which forced the devaluation in the first place, they said.
"I expect a more significant (baht) depreciation to come," said Persaud at JP Morgan.
He said that while the fundamental overvaluation of the baht may have been reversed, an initial deeper decline may be in line.
"I think a devaluation in the order of 30 percent would be resisted but cannot be ruled out. Initially we are going to see a decline much greater than is justified by fundamentals."

Comparing the Thai crisis to the Swedish crown slump in 1992-to-1995, he said devaluation and high interest rates risked imploding the financial sector because of heavy foreign currency borrowings by banks. The currency may need to compensate.
The real test is when exchange controls are removed.
"They haven't really floated it at all yet because they still have a two-tier market," said Douch at BZW.

"Thailand is still going to have to attract capital to balance its books and even at the new lower level of the baht, the current account deficit is 4.5-5.0 pct of GDP," Douch said. "What levels of baht and interest rates are needed to attract that capital is anyone's guess right now."
